item.title: Users vs. independent judges: Comparing perceived authorship and ownership in AI-supported collaborative writing
item.description:
Cyberpsychology Journal of Psychosocial Research on Cyberspace
With the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic and creative settings, understanding how this technology impacts fundamental concepts of authorship and ownership is important to protect learning, maintain academic integrity, and establish clear policies. This study (N = 320; 18 to 44 years old, M = 19.55, SD = 2.39) utilized a 2 (user vs independent judge) x 4 (completely user generated; AI-generated and user edited 4 sentences; user chooses from 3 AI-generated options; completely AI generated) between-subjects design to examine how levels of Large Language Model (LLM) input affect attributions of authorship and ownership by both the users and the independent judges in a collaborative writing task. Findings reveal a significant inverse relationship between the level of LLM input and users’ reported ownership and authorship and a positive relationship between their attributions of ownership and authorship. Additionally, discrepancies emerged between users’ and judges’ attributions, particularly at high and low levels of LLM input, suggesting that third-party evaluators and users may use different factors in allocating credit. Furthermore, this research investigated the role of background factors such as users’ experience with AI, their attitudes toward AI, and their writing level in moderating the relationships between (1) AI input level and attributions of ownership and (2) attributions of ownership and authorship. The findings reveal the need to identify optimal levels of AI integration that support learning without diminishing students’ sense of authorship and to develop assessment strategies that address differences in attributions of ownership by users and independent judges. For policy, the observed differences in attribution demonstrate the complexities of assigning credit and responsibility in AI-assisted creative works.

item.title: Faculty psychological readiness for responsible AI integration in higher education: perceived policy support, teaching engagement, teaching innovation, and professional practice
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Universities are developing policies for artificial intelligence (AI), but less is known about how faculty members' perceptions of policy support relate to their readiness and reported teaching practices. Methods This study examined psychological readiness for responsible AI integration (PRRAI) as a second-order construct with cognitive, affective, and ethical dimensions. We tested its indirect role in the associations between perceived policy support (PPS) and teaching engagement, teaching innovation behavior, and responsible AI professional practice. A cross-sectional survey conducted from June to August 2025 yielded 374 eligible responses from faculty members at 18 higher education institutions in Jiangsu Province, China. Results Structural equation modeling identified positive associations between PPS and PRRAI and between PRRAI and all three outcomes. The PPS-PRRAI coefficient was moderate (β = 0.52); a 1-SD increase in PPS corresponded to approximately 0.35 points on the five-point PRRAI scale. Indirect effects were significant for each outcome. After accounting for PRRAI, the direct association with PPS remained significant for responsible practice but not for engagement or innovation. AI literacy strengthened the PPS-PRRAI association, whereas teaching experience weakened the PRRAI-innovation association. Sensitivity analyses by primary AI referent and institution-clustered standard errors produced the same substantive pattern. Discussion Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings concern perceived support and statistical associations rather than effects of actual policies or interventions.

item.title: Competing cognitive pathways associated with generative AI tool use and self-reported critical thinking in higher education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has raised concerns about its relationship with students’ critical thinking, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Offloading Theory, this study examined the competing indirect associations between GenAI tool use and self-reported critical thinking through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading. It also investigated the sequential indirect association involving both mediators to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cognitive-regulatory processes associated with GenAI-supported learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 378 undergraduate students from 10 universities in Jiangsu Province of China. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). Bias-corrected bootstrap analysis with 5,000 resamples was performed to examine direct, indirect, and total associations, as well as to compare the magnitudes of the competing indirect pathways. Results GenAI tool use was positively associated with self-regulated learning (β = 0.431, p < 0.001) and cognitive offloading (β = 0.390, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was positively associated with critical thinking (β = 0.368, p < 0.001), whereas cognitive offloading was negatively associated with critical thinking (β = −0.409, p < 0.001). Self-regulated learning was also negatively associated with cognitive offloading (β = −0.318, p < 0.001). The direct association between GenAI tool use and critical thinking was not statistically significant (β = −0.059, p = 0.316). Bootstrap analysis identified a positive indirect association through self-regulated learning (B = 0.147, 95% CI [0.096, 0.212]), a negative indirect association through cognitive offloading (B = −0.148, 95% CI [−0.219, −0.092]), and a positive sequential indirect association through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading (B = 0.052, 95% CI [0.030, 0.088]). The total association was not statistically significant, and the two single-mediator indirect associations did not differ significantly in magnitude. Conclusion The relationship between GenAI tool use and critical thinking may be more complex than a uniformly beneficial or detrimental association. The findings reveal the coexistence of positive and negative indirect associations involving self-regulatory processes and cognitive offloading, highlighting the relevance of self-regulated learning in understanding how students engage with GenAI-supported learning. These results underscore the importance of supporting students’ self-regulatory capacities while encouraging thoughtful engagement with AI-generated information. Given the cross-sectional design and self-reported measures, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationships among these constructs and their implications for critical thinking development.

item.title: When predictive models inherit and amplify educational inequity: an intersectional fairness analysis and mitigation study on large-scale learning data
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Machine learning models increasingly predict student outcomes and guide support, yet their fairness across intersecting groups remains underexamined. We assessed fairness in pass/fail prediction across gender and disability, with socioeconomic deprivation as a third dimension. Methods We analyzed 31,482 enrolment records from 27,814 students in the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). We used bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests to assess pass-rate disparities, trained a gradient-boosted ensemble without protected attributes, and compared in-processing and post-processing mitigation using the equal-opportunity gap (difference in true-positive rates) and balanced accuracy. Results Disabled male students had a 34.4% pass rate versus 48.9% among non-disabled female students, a 14.5-percentage-point gap. The model produced a 20.1-point equal-opportunity gap, most disadvantaging students with the lowest observed pass rate. The estimated disparity amplification factor was 1.22 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.91–1.53). Post-processing threshold optimization reduced the equal-opportunity gap by 54% (paired bootstrap 95% CI excluded zero), with no statistically detectable change in balanced accuracy. Post-processing yielded a smaller observed gap than in-processing, although the difference was not statistically significant. Discussion Excluding protected attributes left substantial disparities in student outcome predictions. Intersectional auditing can reveal disparities that single-attribute analyses may overlook.

item.title: How generative artificial intelligence affects college students' learning satisfaction: an analysis based on the chain mediation model
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is profoundly reshaping the learning ecosystem in higher education, yet the mechanisms through which it influences learning experiences remain to be empirically validated. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Protection Motivation Theory, and self-regulated learning theory, this study examines whether AI risk avoidance and self-regulated learning ability mediate the relationship between GenAI adoption orientation and learning satisfaction, both individually and in a serial chain. Survey data are collected from 1,828 students at nine undergraduate universities in Northeast China. The questionnaire included four adapted scales: GenAI adoption orientation, AI risk avoidance, self-regulated learning ability, and learning satisfaction, all rated on a five-point Likert scale. Results indicated that GenAI adoption orientation had no significant direct association with learning satisfaction. Instead, its relationship with satisfaction is mediated by AI risk avoidance and SRL ability. The indirect effect through AI risk avoidance is the largest (estimate = 0.407); the chain indirect effect is also significant (estimate = 0.155, 95% CI [0.039, 0.298]). These findings suggest that technology adoption alone may not guarantee positive learning experiences. Students' attention to AI-related risks and their active regulation of learning are important pathways through which GenAI adoption orientation is associated with satisfaction. The serial mediation effect of these two variables reveals the underlying transmission mechanism: GenAI adoption is associated with greater awareness of AI-related risks, which is in turn associated with more proactive employment of self-regulated strategies and higher learning satisfaction. This study provides empirical evidence for universities to balance effectiveness enhancement and risk guidance when advancing GenAI applications in education.

item.title: Effects of generative AI on self-regulated learning and the incremental contributions of instructional interventions: evidence from a meta-analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Self-regulated learning (SRL) is a core competency essential to students' autonomous learning and their sustainable development. Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) offers new possibilities for supporting SRL. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of Gen-AI and the added value of accompanying instructional interventions remain insufficiently explored. Methods This meta-analysis synthesizes 26 independent studies published between 2023 and 2026, contributing 76 effect sizes, and employs a three-level random-effects model to examine two separate comparative frameworks. Of the included studies, 18 compared Gen-AI-supported learning with learning without AI, while 10 compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with Gen-AI used alone. Two studies provided effect sizes for both types of comparisons. Results In the first framework, we separately compared standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions with the no-AI learning condition, examining their overall effects on SRL. Standalone Gen-AI produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect on students' SRL (ḡ = 0.508, 95% CI [0.261, 0.755]), whereas Gen-AI combined with structured instructional interventions produces a statistically significant moderate positive effect (ḡ= 0.788, 95% CI [0.579, 0.996]). Although the latter yields a larger estimated effect, the difference between the two estimated effects was not statistically significant (Q between = 2.887, df = 1, p = 0.089). These findings suggest that both standalone Gen-AI and Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions can improve students' SRL relative to learning without AI, but do not establish that combining Gen-AI with instructional interventions is significantly more effective than using Gen-AI alone. In the second framework, we directly compared Gen-AI combined with instructional interventions against Gen-AI alone to examine the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. The results revealed a statistically significant moderate positive incremental effect of instructional interventions (ḡ= 0.528, 95% CI [0.359, 0.697]), indicating that instructional interventions provided additional benefits for students' SRL beyond those associated with Gen-AI use alone. Discussion Overall, this study distinguishes between the overall effects of Gen-AI-supported learning relative to no-AI conditions and the incremental contribution of instructional interventions when Gen-AI is already being used. These findings provide empirical evidence for educators, instructional designers, and future research.

item.title: Literacy among contemporary college students based on SEM self-efficacy, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, university students’ digital literacy (DL) has become an important concern in higher education. Drawing on social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this study examined the association between artificial intelligence literacy (AIL) and DL and the parallel mediating roles of information literacy self-efficacy (ILSE), SRL, and learning motivation (LM). Methods A questionnaire survey recruited university students in mainland China and yielded 504 cases for analysis. Measures included adapted versions of the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, a 16-item self-report DL scale covering eight domains, the Chinese-revised Information Literacy Self-Efficacy Scale, the Learners’ Self-Regulated Learning Ability Self-Report Scale, and the motivation section of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0, AMOS 26.0, and semopy 2.3.11. Results AIL showed a positive direct association with DL after all three mediators were included simultaneously (B = 0.233, 95% CI [0.114, 0.363]). The specific indirect effects through ILSE, SRL, and LM were 0.097 (95% CI [0.046, 0.168]), 0.054 (95% CI [0.010, 0.109]), and 0.077 (95% CI [0.027, 0.144]), respectively. None of the confidence intervals included zero. Discussion The findings inform the design of digital learning tasks in higher education, including guided AI skills practice, feedback on challenging tasks, support for goal setting and progress monitoring, and connections to students’ academic interests and future careers. The cross-sectional design and nonprobability sampling limit causal inference and generalizability.

item.title: Teacher self-efficacy in Teacher-AI collaboration: a systematic review
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Although research on Teacher Self-efficacy in Teacher-AI collaboration (TSE-AI) has increased significantly in recent years, no systematic literature synthesis or theoretical integration yet exists. Following PRISMA guidelines and using a thematic synthesis approach, this review examined 59 eligible studies from five databases to clarify how TSE-AI is conceptualized and operationalized across educational levels and AI application scenarios, and to identify its roles as antecedent, mediator, and outcome. The review identified three instrument types, most grounded in Bandura’s social cognitive theory: adapted Teacher Efficacy Scales, domain-specific AI self-efficacy scales, such as the Teacher Artificial Intelligence Competence Self-Efficacy (TAICS) scale, and technology self-efficacy scales. To date, none have been validated as a standard reference, reflecting heterogeneity in measurement approaches. Building on this body of work, the review systematically mapped the paths linking TSE-AI to teachers’psychological and behavioral variables. The construct is conceptualized not as a static trait but as a dynamic, context-sensitive integration of operational and pedagogical efficacy, centered on teachers’beliefs in critically evaluating AI outputs and engaging in joint pedagogical decision-making. This review identified a bidirectional relationship between TSE-AI and Teacher-AI collaboration, the impact of which depends on efficacy calibration: appropriately calibrated efficacy ensures that these beliefs translate into effective collaboration, while exaggerated efficacy may lead to overreliance, potentially undermining teachers’ core instructional and classroom management skills. Directions for future research are discussed.

item.title: Evolving role of educators in higher education: an interview study on three perspectives
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Existing research on AI in higher education has emphasized digital competencies and technology integration, however, less attention has been paid to how changing educator roles are understood across stakeholder groups and shaped by institutional conditions. This qualitative study examines how educators, students, and educational developers construct the evolving role of educators in response to educational technologies, including generative AI, and how these changes are shaped by emotional responses and institutional conditions. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 participants, the study employs inductive reflexive thematic analysis within a contextualist, interpretive framework, using interactionist role theory and, to a lesser extent, control-value theory to interpret role changes and emotional responses to technology, respectively. The findings indicate that the educator role is being renegotiated rather than replaced. Technology was predominantly framed as assistance rather than substitution, while educators remained positioned as responsible for pedagogical judgment, ethical oversight, and human guidance. Emotional responses to technology were mixed and often shaped by uncertainty, trust, and perceived control. Role adaptation was also described as strongly mediated by institutional conditions, including workload, large classes, research–teaching tensions, and uneven engagement with professional development. The paper contributes by shifting attention from technology adoption alone to the interactional, emotional, and institutional processes through which the educator’s role is being reworked in higher education.

item.title: Transforming Diabetes Education: A Systematic Review of Innovative and Evolving Digital Technologies
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
Diabetes education is essential for clinical outcomes, yet conventional approaches remain constrained by limited scalability, personalization and sustained engagement. Existing reviews have examined individual technologies, with limited integration of pedagogical and behavioral perspectives. Following PRISMA guidelines, this systematic review synthesized 40 studies to comparatively evaluate Innovative and Evolving digital technologies for diabetes education. Three categories predominated: chatbots/conversational agents (58%), game-based learning (GBL; 25%) and extended reality (XR; 17%). XR supported immersive training and skill acquisition; GBL encompassed serious games and gamification for experiential learning and engagement; and chatbots ranged from rule-based systems for standardized information delivery to LLM-based systems offering flexible, potentially personalized interaction. Personalization involved educational adaptation, data integration and memory, while engagement strategies included game mechanics, anthropomorphic agents and accessible platforms. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), with 85% of studies rated as high quality. However, clinical effectiveness evidence remains limited: 85% of studies were exploratory, descriptive, pilot, or quasi-experimental, whereas only 15% were randomized controlled trials, with few assessing long-term outcomes. Overall, evidence suggests benefits for knowledge, skills and short-term behaviors but highlights limited theoretical grounding, pedagogical depth and individualized adaptation.

item.title: The erosion of necessity pressure: how generative AI reshapes the conditions of cognitive engagement in higher education
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
This study examines how continuous access to generative artificial intelligence reshapes cognitive engagement in higher education. Rather than focusing only on learning outcomes, efficiency, or cognitive offloading, the study investigates how persistent AI availability may influence the conditions under which students perceive continued independent thinking as necessary. Drawing on a qualitative, theory-building study of 25 undergraduate students in Shenzhen, China, the study collected data through 18 face-to-face interviews and 7 asynchronous written interviews with students who regularly use generative AI in their academic work. The findings develop the concept of epistemic insurance, referring to the expectation that unresolved difficulty can be externally resolved at relatively low cost. This condition can weaken necessity pressure, making sustained cognitive engagement more conditional and allowing task completion to outpace independent understanding in some situations. However, this mechanism is not deterministic. Students who deliberately delay, restrict, or selectively use AI can preserve greater independent engagement, identifying self-binding as an important boundary condition. The study contributes a process-level explanation of how the continuous availability of generative AI may influence when students persist with difficulty, when they externalize cognitive effort, and how this shapes the relationship between task completion and independent understanding.

item.title: Researcherly Dispositions and Teachers’ Artificial Intelligence TPACK Development: A Two-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study of Adult Intellectual Development
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming classroom teaching, yet two-wave repeated cross-sectional evidence on how K-12 teachers develop the knowledge that underpins intelligent performance with AI remains scarce. Our two-year study across 29 schools thus explored the associations between university-facilitated teacher action research and the development of artificial intelligence technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK), a domain-specific form of intelligence-as-knowledge in teaching. Data were collected using questionnaires on research-related dispositions and AI-TPACK with 285 participants in Year 1 and 200 participants in Year 2. Structural equation modeling suggested that the associations of teachers’ research consumption and production with their AI-TPACK differed between the two waves, possibly reflecting shifting program task requirements, whereas research attitude served as a stable predictor. The findings yield preliminary evidence regarding linkages between action research and teachers’ AI-TPACK, and highlight the differences in these associations across the two waves. Considered from the perspective of adult intellectual development, these results suggest that knowledge in professional practice might be sustained by opportunities to convert inquiry into produced knowledge, refining accounts of how expertise with intelligent technologies develops.

item.title: Academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency among university students: academic anxiety as a mediator and teacher emotional support as a moderator
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI has become increasingly integrated into university students’ academic writing, offering substantial support while also raising concerns about excessive reliance on AI. Understanding how support within the teaching environment relates to this reliance may help inform educational efforts to address AI dependency. This study examined the psychological and environmental factors associated with AI dependency in academic writing, focusing on academic writing self-efficacy, academic anxiety, and teacher emotional support. Methods Using cross-sectional survey data from 1,012 university students across four regions of China, mediation and moderated mediation effects were tested through structural equation modeling. Results The results showed that lower academic writing self-efficacy was associated with greater AI dependency both directly and indirectly through higher academic anxiety. Although teacher emotional support was negatively correlated with academic anxiety overall, its conditional association with anxiety varied across levels of academic writing self-efficacy: it was negative at lower levels but positive at higher levels. The negative conditional indirect association between academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency through academic anxiety was also weaker at higher levels of teacher emotional support. Discussion These findings suggest that academic anxiety may help explain the association between academic writing self-efficacy and AI dependency and highlight a potential compensatory role of teacher emotional support among students with lower writing self-efficacy. They underscore the value of considering both students’ writing self-efficacy and support within the teaching environment when developing educational approaches to address excessive reliance on AI in academic writing.

item.title: Acceptance beliefs predict undergraduates’ self-assessed research competency but not their instructor-assessed coursework
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Self-assessment is central to self-regulated learning, yet people’s insight into their own ability is moderate at best, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may weaken it further by making work feel fluent whatever the learner has mastered. This study asked how closely undergraduates’ ratings of their own research competency correspond to instructors’ assessment of their coursework and which beliefs go with each. Methods Over one semester, management undergraduates at four institutions in Guangdong, China, completed two research assignments scored by their instructors on a common four-dimension rubric. Intact classes were assigned, without randomisation, to structured GenAI guidance (a guidebook, tutorials, demonstrations, and briefs specifying which steps AI could assist with) or to a comparison condition with the same assignments and conventional guidance; GenAI tools were available to both. Rubric scores covered complete class rosters (n = 284), and the questionnaire measures a linked pre-post panel (n = 169). Results The 19-item self-rating was dominated by a general factor, and its correlation with instructor-assessed performance was small (r = 0.04, 95% CI [−0.12, 0.21]; the interval excludes moderate but not small positive correlations), including when content areas were matched. The hypothesised association between change in perceived usefulness and the self-rating did not survive conservative record linkage and is treated as unsupported. In exploratory analyses, post-test perceived usefulness, ease of use, and attitude were positively associated with the self-rating (b = 0.38 to 0.44, p < 0.001) in both conditions and after weighting for attrition, and none showed a significant positive association with instructor-assessed performance. In all three institutions with usable rubric scores, the class given structured guidance scored higher on the second assignment, by 0.57 points on the 16-point rubric when pooled (d = 0.24), most clearly on analytical depth. Discussion With six non-randomised classes, non-blind single-rater scoring, and a covariate measured after the guidance was issued, this contrast is descriptive, not causal. The two outcomes are not equivalent instruments: one is a global self-perception, and the other is an evaluation of AI-assisted work. Within those limits, students’ self-ratings went with their beliefs about the tools and could not stand in for the instructors’ assessment of their coursework.

item.title: Anxiety-calibrated generative-AI feedback for second language writing: the Cognition–Affect Dual-Adaptation model
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can now deliver instant, detailed written corrective feedback on second language (L2) writing, but current systems deliver essentially the same message to every learner. We argue that this one-size-fits-all design neglects robust evidence that feedback effectiveness depends on learners’ emotional states—particularly writing anxiety. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes the Cognition–Affect Dual-Adaptation (CADA) model, which decomposes GAI feedback into a constant cognitive channel (error identification, explanation, and revision suggestions, identical for all learners) and an affective channel calibrated to the learner’s current anxiety tier (praise framing, mitigation intensity, and strength-first sequencing), with dynamic re-tiering as anxiety changes over time. Unlike existing adaptive-feedback frameworks, which adjust task difficulty or content selection, CADA leaves what is said untouched and adapts how it is said; and unlike ad hoc prompt-based personalization, it specifies the calibration rule, the psychological construct the rule responds to, and the conditions under which the rule itself should change. Integrating control–value theory, social cognitive theory, broaden-and-build theory, and feedback-literacy research, we advance six testable propositions: relative to uniform GAI feedback, CADA-calibrated feedback is predicted to (P1) reduce writing anxiety and (P2) increase writing self-efficacy; (P3) improve writing performance through a chained self-efficacy-to-anxiety mediation; (P4) yield compensatory benefits that are strongest for learners with high baseline anxiety; (P5) increase feedback uptake, which partially mediates performance gains; and (P6) produce self-correcting downward tier migration as within-person anxiety declines. We specify the model’s boundary conditions and a multi-phase research agenda spanning experimental, longitudinal, and process-tracing designs. The model proposes affect-responsive calibration as a candidate first-order design property of GAI writing tools and provides an integrative, falsifiable framework for research on emotion-adaptive feedback in L2 writing. If the propositions hold, emotional fit could become a specifiable, auditable property of every feedback message a learner receives—an outcome within reach of current GAI writing tools.

item.title: AI readiness and indirect associations between AI literacy, TPB-based GAI antecedents, and behavioral intention to use generative AI among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into nursing education. Understanding factors associated with nursing students’ Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) use intention is essential. Aim This study examined the associations of AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents with behavioral intention, and tested whether AI readiness was associated with the indirect pathways in two separate adjusted mediation models. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 650 undergraduate nursing students used the AI Literacy, AI Readiness, and GAI Behavior Influencing Factors scales. Results Mean scores were 64.71 ± 10.84 (AI literacy), 19.34 ± 2.46 (AI readiness), and 20.69 ± 3.68 (behavioral intention). In two separate adjusted mediation models, AI readiness was significantly associated with the indirect pathways from AI literacy (0.012, 95% CI: 0.005–0.020) and TPB-based GAI antecedents (0.013, 95% CI: 0.006–0.022), accounting for 37.5% and 4.2% of the total associations, respectively. Conclusion In two separate adjusted models, AI literacy and TPB-based GAI antecedents were associated with behavioral intention directly and indirectly through AI readiness. These findings represent statistical indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Systematic AI education may be proposed as a potential strategy to promote GAI integration, although this was not tested in the current study.

item.title: Self-regulated learning processes in music composition supported by music-specific generative AI: a microanalytic multiple-case study of Chinese undergraduates
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Music-specific generative AI (MS-AI) can accelerate the production of musical material, while learners still need to set goals, select strategies, monitor progress, and evaluate and revise what is generated. This study examined these processes within Zimmerman’s three-phase model of self-regulated learning (SRL). Methods An explanatory multiple-case study was conducted with three Chinese undergraduate music majors completing a 45-min MS-AI-supported composition task. Data comprised task-embedded SRL microanalysis prompts, full-session video recordings, composition files, and stimulated recall interviews. Results Cross-case analysis identified three contrasting regulatory patterns. Han followed a goal-led pattern, using specific structural criteria, sequenced strategies, and deliberate monitoring to guide targeted revisions. Yuan followed a rule-anchored pattern, monitoring consistently and evaluating material mainly against classroom rules and established stylistic procedures. Jin followed a template-reliant pattern, using broader thematic goals, repeated generation and selection, and fewer targeted revisions. Thirty-one percent of net composing time was independently double-coded (κ = 0.97). Deliberate monitoring occupied 76%, 69%, and 19% of Han’s, Yuan’s, and Jin’s net composing time, respectively. Routine monitoring occupied 19%, 31%, and 77%, and off-task behavior occupied 5%, 0%, and 4%, respectively. Discussion Across the three cases, more specific goals were associated with more deliberate monitoring. Targeted revision was an indicator used to identify deliberate monitoring, so their co-occurrence is descriptive. Deliberate monitoring supported both exploratory revision and rule-based validation. The findings extend SRL microanalysis to real-time composition and identify processes for further study in larger samples and over longer composing periods.

item.title: GenAI-supported self-explanation and its effects on metacognitive monitoring and critical reading comprehension: evidence from two experimental studies
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Generative AI (GenAI) holds considerable promise for supporting self-explanation and self-regulated learning (SRL), yet little is known about how different forms of GenAI-based support influence learning and metacognitive outcomes. Grounded in Zimmerman’s three-phase SRL model, the present research examined the effects of GenAI-based feedback and prompts embedded in self-explanation activities on critical reading comprehension, metacognitive monitoring, and cognitive load across two sequential experiments with Chinese university students. Study 1 (N = 119) compared three conditions in an integrative self-explanation context: self-explanation with personalized GenAI feedback (SE + FB), self-explanation only (SE), and a reading-only control. The SE + FB group demonstrated significantly better critical reading comprehension than both comparison groups and higher germane cognitive load than the control group. It also showed a negative monitoring bias (underestimation), whereas the comparison groups showed positive biases (overestimation), although absolute monitoring accuracy did not differ significantly across conditions. Study 2 (N = 113) compared scaffolded, standard, and no prompts provided before error-based self-explanations. Scaffolded prompts significantly improved self-explanation quality relative to both comparison groups and metacognitive monitoring accuracy relative to the no-prompt group. However, no significant differences in critical reading comprehension were observed across conditions. Together, these findings suggest that different forms of GenAI-based support for self-explanation may contribute to distinct cognitive and metacognitive outcomes, highlighting the importance of aligning support with specific learning activities to facilitate critical reading and self-regulated learning.

item.title: An online classroom teaching evaluation method integrating the wisdom of domain experts with the intelligent capabilities of large language models
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Online classrooms have become an important teaching modality due to their real-time interactivity. However, existing teaching evaluation methods rely heavily on subjective observations and post-class questionnaires, resulting in limited efficiency, objectivity, and timeliness. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for multimodal teaching evaluation, but their susceptibility to hallucinations may undermine evaluation reliability and decision validity. Integrating expert knowledge with LLM capabilities offers a promising solution, yet effective human-AI collaboration remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study proposes an online classroom teaching evaluation framework comprising a multimodal evaluation indicator system and a human-AI collaborative assessment method integrating LLMs with expert intelligence. The framework was validated through case studies, questionnaires, and interviews. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework generates reliable and interpretable teaching evaluation reports. Teachers and learners perceive these reports as valuable for analyzing teaching behaviors, optimizing instructional content, and improving learning experiences. This study contributes to the development of human-AI collaborative teaching evaluation and provides practical guidance for achieving more objective, efficient, and evidence-based online classroom assessment.

item.title: Beyond Giving Answers: Scaffolding Critical Thinking with Stage-Structured Generative AI Feedback in Introductory Programming
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence can support programming learning, but complete solutions may reduce opportunities to practice critical thinking. This study examined a pedagogical agent guided by the Trigger-Process-Respond framework, which organized questioning, comparison, evidence requests, and reflection across debugging, code review, and post-task reflection. In a six-week quasi-experiment, 60 first-year computer science students in two intact classes at a Chinese university completed three sequential programming tasks. One class used the agent, and the other received conventional instructor feedback. Critical thinking was assessed with the Chinese version of the California Critical Thinking Skills Test, and dialogue records documented students’ reasoning responses. In these two classes, the agent-supported class had higher posttest scores after adjustment for pretest scores. Within the fixed feedback sequences, questioning was followed by more analytical responses, comparison by more evaluative responses, and evidence requests by more argumentative responses. Exploratory analyses linked reflection feedback with reasoning in the next task, particularly between the first two tasks. These findings suggest that stage-structured generative AI feedback can engage students in reasoning during supported programming dialogue.

item.title: Longitudinal associations among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence in generative AI use
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into university students’ information seeking and problem solving, individuals’ curiosity, trust in GenAI, and functional dependence on it may interact over the course of continued use. However, the longitudinal relationships among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence, as well as their potential transmission mechanisms, remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on information gap theory, a cognitive resource perspective, and the trust and reliance framework in automation, this study adopted a three-wave longitudinal design and a cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) to examine the dynamic relationships among curiosity, Human–AI trust, and functional dependence on GenAI among university students. A total of 952 Chinese university students participated in three waves of data collection at approximately one-year intervals (M age (T3) = 20.35 years). The results showed consistent bidirectional positive cross-lagged associations between Human–AI trust and functional dependence across both time intervals. In contrast, the relationship between curiosity and functional dependence was temporally asymmetric: T1 curiosity positively predicted T2 functional dependence, whereas T2 functional dependence positively predicted T3 curiosity; the corresponding reverse paths were not significant. In addition, two significant longitudinal indirect pathways through functional dependence were identified: T1 Human–AI trust was indirectly associated with T3 curiosity through T2 functional dependence, and T1 curiosity was indirectly associated with T3 Human–AI trust through T2 functional dependence. These findings suggest that functional dependence may serve as an important behavioral pathway linking curiosity and Human–AI trust, and provide longitudinal evidence for understanding how curiosity, trust, and functional dependence interact over time during university students’ continued use of GenAI.

item.title: Identifying predictors of stress biomarkers in secondary school students using machine learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
During their academic journey, especially between ages 11 and 15, secondary school students often face heightened stress due to increased academic demands, responsibilities, and future concerns, posing a significant risk to students’ well-being and academic success. To support students’ healthy development, it is crucial to understand the primary predictors of physiological stress markers in secondary school students’ lives. Although previous research has identified several individual predictors, little is known about how a broad range of psychosocial, demographic, and behavioral characteristics jointly contribute to the prediction of physiological stress biomarkers in adolescents. To model how up to 59 variables describing adolescents’ (N = 83; Mage = 13.72 years; 48% girls) social, psychological, and school-related factors predicted their physiological stress markers (cortisol, alpha-amylase, oxidative stress, telomere length) in a cross-sectional study, a machine learning approach was adopted. Random forests and Lasso models were fitted for each biomarker using cross-validation. Random Forest models predicting salivary alpha-amylase (p = 0.006) and Lasso models predicting telomere length (p = 0.005) achieved significantly lower prediction errors than the corresponding baseline models. Feature importance analyses indicated avoidance of academic failure as the most important predictor of alpha-amylase, followed by parental support, stress and burnout, inclusion in classroom and social media use. Telomere length was primarily predicted by school track, followed by social media use, gaming, sibling count, and burnout symptoms. The findings identify motivational, demographic, social, and technology-related characteristics as potentially informative predictors of physiological biomarkers. However, the observed relationships should be interpreted as exploratory and model-dependent rather than evidence that individual characteristics act as stressors or protective factors.

item.title: The relationship between LLM usage and critical thinking among college students: the mediating role of task assessment
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective College students are increasingly using Large Language Models (LLMs) in their studies. This study aims to explore the relationship between LLM usage patterns and college students’ critical thinking and further examine the mediating role of task assessment in this relationship, offering implications for teaching design and policy making. Methods Based on the Expectancy-value theory and the convenience sampling method, a survey was conducted among 544 college students through LLM usage pattern scale, task assessment scale and critical thinking scale. The collected data were interpreted through descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with bootstrap, logistic regression and heterogeneity analysis in Stata. Results Measured on a 5-point Likert scale and computed as the mean of their respective items, Explanatory usage of LLM (EU) was strongly positively associated with task value (VAL, involving intrinsic, attainment, and utility value) (r = 0.735, p < 0.001) and Critical Thinking (CT) (r = 0.694, p < 0.001), while VAL was strongly correlated with CT (r = 0.757, p < 0.001). Generative usage of LLM (GU) was positively correlated with VAL (r = 0.287, p < 0.001) and task cost (COST, including effort, opportunity, and psychological cost) (r = 0.558, p < 0.001). EU highly predicted VAL (β = 0.707, p < 0.001) and CT (β = 0.305, p < 0.001) and Generative Usage of LLM (GU) strongly predicted COST (β = 0.561, p < 0.001). VAL significantly predicted CT (β = 0.565, p < 0.001) and mediated the EU-CT relationship (β = 0.400, p < 0.001), accounting for 56.74% of the total effect. High-EU groups showed higher CT and VAL than low-EU groups (all p < 0.001), and Explorers (high EU, low GU) reported the lowest COST (2.74). Higher VAL reduced the possibility to become Shortcut (low EU, high GU) members by 59.3% (Odd Ratio, OR = 0.407, p < 0.001), while higher COST increased them by 130.7% (OR = 2.307, p < 0.001). Conclusion (1) EU is positively associated with CT both directly and indirectly through higher task value, with the indirect path accounting for 56.74% of the total association. (2) GU shows no significant overall association with CT, but is substantially associated with higher task cost, producing opposite indirect effects through value and cost. (3) High-EU Students show stronger CT, while Explorers report the lowest burden; Low-EU groups perform worse. These findings can help teachers and schools better understand college students’ learning behaviors in the artificial intelligence era, design more valuable learning tasks and enhance students’ critical thinking abilities.

item.title: Research on the correlation of artificial intelligence painting tools with adolescents’ art learning motivation and creative effect
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Digital aesthetic education and mental health of children and adolescents are important research topics in the field of public health. The popularity of artificial intelligence painting tools has reshaped the form of art education, but its relationship with adolescents’ art learning motivation, creative self-efficacy and mental health literacy has not yet reached an empirical conclusion. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 342 adolescents assigned to an observation group (AI painting tools, n = 174) and a control group (traditional art tools, n = 168) by prior painting tool use. The Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), Creative Self-efficacy Scale (ASES), and Mental Health Scale for Chinese Adolescents (MHS-CA) were used for assessment. Propensity scores were estimated via multivariable logistic regression, and stabilized inverse probability weighting (IPTW) balanced baseline demographic, art background and learning frequency covariates; standardized mean differences (SMD) before and after weighting were reported. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression explored the nonlinear dose–response relationship between weekly AI painting duration and outcomes. Three knots at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles were chosen based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), with nonlinear p values and 95% CIs of inflection points reported. Multivariate hierarchical covariance analysis, Pearson correlation and Bootstrap mediation models were applied for further analyses. Between-group comparisons were performed on stabilized IPTW-weighted data. Weighted means and robust Huber-White standard errors were calculated. Categorical and continuous variables were compared using the χ 2 test and weighted t -test, respectively. Results After IPTW weighting, the scores of total motivation, intrinsic motivation and creative self-efficacy in the observation group were higher than those in the control group, and the differences between the two groups were statistically significant (t = 6.19, 5.91 and 6.47, all p < 0.001, Cohen’s d was 0.67, 0.64 and 0.70, respectively). Retrospective observation data show that the weekly use time of intelligent painting tools is positively correlated with adolescents’ creative self-efficacy in fine arts (β = 0.462, p < 0.001). The bias-corrected Bootstrap 95% confidence interval shows that there is a significant indirect effect between artistic psychological resilience and aesthetic concentration, and the indirect effect accounts for 41.36% of the total effect. According to the observation data, tool use is related to the lower probability of adolescents’ high art learning burnout (defined by the upper quartile) (OR = 0.429, 95% CI: 0.287–0.642, p < 0.01). Conclusion This retrospective study shows that the use of artificial intelligence painting tools is positively related to adolescents’ art learning motivation and creative self-efficacy, and is related to a low probability of art learning burnout. The above correlation results need to be further verified by prospective cohort study or randomized controlled trial. This study provides a preliminary empirical reference for adolescent digital health aesthetic education, mental health and public health intervention.

item.title: Competency‑based and emotional predictors of pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards the responsible use of Generative AI
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into initial teacher education requires an understanding not only of how frequently these tools are used, but also of the factors that shape their responsible adoption. This study examines how pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards responsible GenAI use is configured, identifying the competency-based resources and usage‑related variables that underpin it, as well as the role of anxiety across the dimensions assessed. A total of 298 pre‑service teachers from two Spanish universities participated, completing a validated 25‑item instrument comprising five dimensions: attitudes towards the use of AI for employability, digital flow in the responsible and safe use of AI, creativity to use AI responsibly, anxiety about using AI in future work contexts, and responsible use of AI for employability. Robust group comparisons, hierarchical regressions, and a network analysis with hierarchical clustering were conducted. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the instrument’s five‑factor structure. Creativity (β = 0.42) and digital flow (β = 0.37) emerged as the strongest predictors of responsible use, whereas usage frequency made no unique positive contribution. Anxiety was higher among women and younger participants; in the regression model it was associated with more favourable attitudes and higher digital flow, and with lower creativity only when these were controlled (a suppression effect). It occupied a peripheral position within the correlation network. The findings are synthesised in an exploratory two‑path empirical model that requires confirmatory testing. Initial teacher education may therefore benefit from fostering creative GenAI‑based experiences while deliberately addressing the emotional dimension of learning these technologies.

item.title: Cognitive engagement of early childhood learners with AI avatars as learning companions in the metaverse: an ICAP-Based analysis
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
As digital technologies become increasingly embedded in early childhood education (ECE), understanding their developmental implications has become more urgent. Although systematic reviews have examined emerging technologies in ECE, the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and metaverse remains underexplored. Furthermore, existing studies have rarely examined how relational and embodied digital interactions contribute to deeper forms of learning among young children. Therefore, this study investigated the cognitive engagement of preschoolers interacting with AI-powered avatars within a developmentally appropriate metaverse environment. Using a qualitative-dominant mixed methods design, 30 preschool-aged children completed three dialogic learning sessions, with interaction transcripts, behavioral observations, system logs, and field notes analyzed through ICAP-based coding and supporting quantitative comparisons. Findings revealed that active engagement was the dominant mode, but over time, participation increasingly shifted toward constructive and interactive forms. This progression was supported by the constellation of spatial interactivity, narrative immersion, and embodied presence afforded by the metaverse, alongside the relational adaptivity of AI avatars through memory-based dialogue. These results highlight the potential of AI-driven metaverse to extend early learning by promoting collaborative meaning-making and sustained dialogic participation. Implications for the intentional design of relational AI systems and the development of human-centered metaverse learning environments in ECE are discussed.

item.title: Not Whether but What: A Systematic Review of the Locus of Offloading in Generative AI and Higher-Order Thinking
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reduces the effort of learning tasks, but its effect on students’ higher-order thinking may depend on what is offloaded. This pre-registered systematic review synthesized 26 studies (2024–2026), identified from 4729 records, that measured cognitive load and higher-order thinking in the same higher education sample. Across 21 experimental studies, GenAI conditions most often showed lower load (12 studies) and better higher-order outcomes (14 studies). Lower load coincided with poorer thinking in three studies, none of high quality, and in all three the tool was positioned to perform the target thinking. Most outcomes were self-reports or products created using the available tool, and the only study assessing thinking after the tool was withdrawn found a decline. We propose, as a hypothesis, that offloading supports learning when the tool takes over preparatory work but may undermine it when the tool takes over the thinking the task should exercise.

item.title: Too Much of a Good Thing? The Inverted U-Shaped Effect of Undergraduates’ Generative AI Dependence on Higher-Order Thinking and the Moderating Role of Prompt Engineering Competence
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has attracted sustained attention from educational researchers and practitioners concerning how such tools reshape student learning. Scholars have yet to agree on whether—and, more importantly, under what conditions—GenAI facilitates or inhibits learning. This disagreement persists in part because most researchers conceptualize GenAI use as a single, undifferentiated exposure. Prior scholarship rests on linear assumptions and fails to account for why, at a given level of GenAI dependence, different layers of higher-order thinking respond asymmetrically. Drawing on the too-much-of-a-good-thing (TMGT) metatheory, the expertise reversal effect (ERE) as an interpretive framework—whose implications we test but whose underlying mechanism we do not measure—and Bloom’s revised taxonomy, we hypothesize that GenAI dependence and higher-order thinking ability exhibit an inverted U-shaped relationship. Given that learners’ capacity to steer GenAI outputs shapes the benefits and risks of GenAI reliance, prompt engineering competence (PEC) is modeled as a metacognitive calibration mechanism moderating this curvilinear relationship. Based on 713 valid questionnaires collected from three universities located in the eastern, central, and western regions of China, hierarchical regression and the Sasabuchi–Lind–Mehlum (SLM) formal test confirmed a significant inverted U-shape; students with higher PEC exhibited a rightward-shifted turning point and a flatter descending segment. Robustness checks based on Winsorization and 1000-run permutation tests indicated that the main inverted-U effect remained stable, whereas the curvilinear moderation by PEC received more tentative support. Theoretically, we extend TMGT from psychology and management into human–AI cognitive coupling; practically, we offer tentative guidance for setting pedagogical boundaries of GenAI integration and for stratified cultivation of prompt engineering literacy.

item.title: AI-enabled practice feedback and self-regulated learning among Chinese applied piano undergraduates: a three-wave cross-lagged study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Advanced piano performance is built on long hours of largely unsupervised practice, and what separates productive from unproductive practice is the quality of the monitoring and adjustment the learner brings to the room. Artificial intelligence practice applications now report pitch, rhythm and timing errors automatically, but it is not known whether such feedback strengthens self-regulated learning or moves monitoring from the learner to the software. Methods This study followed 452 applied piano undergraduates from three institutions across one semester, with assessments at weeks 2, 10, and 18. Of these, 385 completed all three waves and form the analysis sample for the panel model. At each wave students reported their use of AI-enabled practice feedback, their self-regulated learning, and their metacognitive offloading, and they kept weekly practice logs. Confirmatory factor analysis, longitudinal measurement invariance testing, a three-wave cross-lagged panel model with cross-interval equality constraints, a within-between decomposition, and regression on the end-of-semester performance score were combined. Results Feedback use and self-regulated learning predicted each other across waves (beta = 0.137 and 0.136, both p < 0.001). Feedback use also predicted more metacognitive offloading (beta = 0.219), which in turn predicted less self-regulated learning (beta = −0.138, p < 0.001). Through offloading, the indirect pathway was negative [ab = −0.029, 95% CI (−0.041, −0.017)] while the direct pathway stayed positive. End-of-semester performance was predicted by self-regulated learning (beta = 0.311) and negatively by offloading (beta = −0.116), but not directly by feedback use. Discussion AI-enabled practice feedback and self-regulated learning reinforce each other over a semester, with the enabling association resting on stable differences between students, and the wave-to-wave fluctuation running mainly from regulation to later feedback use. Part of that gain is given back when the learner transfers monitoring to the tool. Practice systems should require the learner to judge the passage before the system reports, so that feedback scaffolds self-regulation instead of replacing it.

item.title: Community of inquiry presences, GenAI use, and metacognitive regulation in GenAI-mediated L2 learning: evidence from SEM and fsQCA
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made language practice readily accessible. Yet access alone tells us little about how learners engage with the technology and regulate their learning. Drawing on the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, this study examined the relationships among perceived social presence (SP), cognitive presence (CP), teaching presence (TP), GenAI use for second language (L2) learning (GLU), L2 speaking self-efficacy (LSS), student engagement (SE), and metacognitive regulation tendency (MRT). Survey data from 1,160 Chinese university students across seven universities were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). SEM revealed strong interrelationships among the three CoI presences and a positive association between their shared dimension and GLU. Within the hypothesized model, GLU was indirectly associated with MRT through LSS ( β = 0.108) and SE ( β = 0.477). However, these indirect associations were sensitive to alternative model specifications, particularly the pathway involving student engagement. fsQCA identified the joint presence of SP, CP, and TP as a configuration associated with high GLU (consistency = 0.943; coverage = 0.853). High MRT was associated with two configurations, GLU combined with SE and LSS combined with SE, both highlighting engagement as a core condition. These findings extend the CoI framework to GenAI-mediated L2 learning and underscore the relevance of learners’ psychological experiences to self-reported metacognitive regulation. GenAI may make learning opportunities abundant, while engagement could help explain how learners relate those opportunities to regulating their learning.

item.title: Leakage-aware AutoGluon and explainable AI for autism screening-label analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) requires early detection and lifelong support, yet clinical assessment is lengthy and difficult to scale. Machine learning can accelerate screening, but most models remain opaque to clinicians and caregivers. Methods Three public datasets were harmonized ( n = 3,743; 1,991 positive and 1,752 negative screening labels) and split into training (2,395), validation (599), and untouched test (749) sets. AutoGluon was benchmarked against seven classical learners under three feature settings: A1 -A10 items alone, A1 -A10 plus demographic/context variables, and demographic/context variables alone. A circularity audit, Kernel SHAP, rule baselines, and leave-one-source-out (LOSO) validation examined what the models learned. Results A simple A1 -A10 threshold reproduced 100% of labels in two sources and 82.57% in the third. On the test set, the full model achieved 98.93% accuracy (95% CI: 98.13% -99.60%) and a macro-F1 of 0.9893 (95% CI: 0.9812 -0.9960), compared with 0.8478 for A1 -A10 alone and 0.7519 for demographics alone. SHAP rankings were stable across background samples (Spearman ρ = 0.8588) and consistent between autism_screening and toddler_2018 ( ρ = 0.8559), but diverged for data_csv ( ρ = 0.1618 and 0.1118). Rule baselines reached a macro-F1 of 1.0000 in autism_screening and toddler_2018; AutoGluon matched the toddler_2018 rule but did not improve on the autism_screening rule. In data_csv, it outperformed an item-sum baseline (0.9898 vs. 0.8142). LOSO macro-F1 ranged from 0.5566 to 0.9473. Conclusion Near-ceiling performance reflects reconstruction of screening labels rather than independent clinical prediction. The framework offers a transparent tool for auditing screening models; external clinical validation is required before real-world use.

item.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and occupational well-being in higher education management: evidence from universities in Guangzhou
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Universities are increasingly introducing artificial intelligence (AI) tools into administrative and managerial work. Yet evidence on how AI adoption relates to occupational well-being in higher education management remains fragmented. Building on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and contemporary technostress scholarship, this study examines direct, indirect, and conditional associations between AI adoption and occupational well-being in university management in Guangzhou. Methods The cross-sectional questionnaire dataset contained 320 complete records and was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with a two-stage interaction specification and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results AI adoption was positively associated with technostress, which was negatively associated with occupational well-being. Neither the direct AI adoption-well-being association nor the conditional total association at mean organizational support was statistically significant. The negative indirect association through technostress was significant at that support level. Perceived organizational support was positively associated with well-being and with a weaker negative technostress-well-being association. The model explained 23.04% of technostress variance and 10.69% of well-being variance. Discussion These results support a statistical stress pathway but do not establish a direct well-being benefit of AI adoption. Cross-sectional associations do not establish causal mechanisms. The study contributes an occupational well-being perspective to AI-enabled university administration and identifies training, workload redesign, and organizational support as priorities for future evaluation.

item.title: Gen-AI knowledge and students’ acceptance orientation: the serial mediating roles of application competence and ethical awareness
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) is increasingly used in higher education, yet the relationships among students’ knowledge of its limitations, application competence, ethical awareness, and acceptance orientation remain insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study used convenience sampling to recruit 483 university students from three universities in Guangxi, China, between October and December 2025. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariate-adjusted observed-variable path analysis were conducted to examine the proposed associations. The hypothesized serial indirect association between Gen-AI knowledge and acceptance orientation through application competence and ethical awareness was statistically significant ( B = 0.035, 95% bootstrap CI [0.020, 0.055]). The individual indirect associations through application competence ( B = 0.082, 95% bootstrap CI [0.050, 0.121]) and ethical awareness ( B = 0.062, 95% bootstrap CI [0.032, 0.098]) were also significant. In contrast, the direct association between Gen-AI knowledge and acceptance orientation was not statistically significant after adjustment for the mediators ( B = 0.026, 95% CI [−0.032, 0.083]). Exploratory alternative-ordering analyses indicated that other theoretically plausible sequences were also compatible with the data. These findings identify individual and serial indirect associations among dimensions of Gen-AI literacy and acceptance orientation, but do not establish causal or temporal ordering. Longitudinal and intervention-based research is needed to evaluate the direction of these relationships and their implications for educational practice.

item.title: Enhancing Students’ AI Prompt-Engineering Skills and Learning Effectiveness: An Integrated Perspective of AI Readiness and ARCS-Based Learning Motivation
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and its impact on management education in terms of transforming the development of both pedagogical theories and instructional design has drawn significant attention from educators. Prompt engineering has emerged as a critical skill in the era of applying generative AI (GAI) to educational settings. However, this issue is seldom specifically investigated in management education contexts. By taking the use of ChatGPT as a learning support tool in brand management courses as an example, this study investigates how students’ ARCS-based learning motivation and AI readiness may shape their AI prompt-engineering skills and overall learning effectiveness. A total of 196 validated responses acquired via a randomized experimental design utilizing a convenient sampling procedure were used for analysis by using the partial least squares technique. The findings indicate that students’ ARCS-based learning motivation significantly enhances their AI readiness and prompt-engineering skills, thereby increasing their learning effectiveness through interactive GAI-supported learning activities. The implications for both theory and practice are subsequently presented.

item.title: Performance, Perceptions and Productive Behaviors in Generative AI-Supported Personalized Game-Based Cybersecurity Learning: A Sustained Motivation-Enhanced Learning Framework
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
As cybersecurity risks increase, cultivating students’ cybersecurity awareness and skills has become a critical challenge in education. Although digital game-based learning has been used to enhance students’ cybersecurity learning performance, awareness and motivation, customized and static feedback provided in digital games often fail to meet students’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which undermines their persistence and motivation. Therefore, this study integrated a motivation-enhancement mechanism into personalized feedback to stimulate and maintain motivation based on the GAFCC (goal, accessibility, feedback, challenge, and collaboration) model and self-determination theory (SDT), and proposed a motivation-enhanced generative AI-powered personalized feedback (MPF-GenAI) approach to compensate for the shortcomings of the existing feedback mechanisms in terms of adaptability and motivation maintenance. To assess its effectiveness, a quasi-experiment was conducted in a cybersecurity course at an arts-oriented middle school. The results revealed that the proposed approach significantly improved students’ cybersecurity learning performance, awareness, and learning motivation. Learning behavior analysis indicated that the experimental group showed more frequent advice-seeking and return-to-learning behaviors, whereas the control group more often relied on direct-answer-seeking patterns. Students’ learning reflections also indicated that the MPF-GenAI approach effectively enhanced students’ motivation and confidence, and increased their initiative in using GenAI agents to acquire knowledge and seek advice. This study not only proposes a sustained motivation-enhanced learning framework, but also offers actionable insights for frontline teachers to improve students’ learning outcomes and foster learning motivation in classroom practice.

item.title: Balancing scaffolding and agency: how AI story suggestions shape children’s writing processes and narrative development
item.description:
Journal of the Learning Sciences
Background Generative AI can support children’s writing while raising concerns about agency and authorship. This study examines how AI-generated story suggestions and structured non-generative prompts shape children’s writing processes, engagement, and narrative outcomes.Methods An exploratory comparative case study involved 19 multilingual children aged 8–14 across two four-day writing workshops. Participants used either SmartStory, which provided AI-generated story suggestions, or StepStory, which offered structured prompts without generative content. Mixed-methods analyses combined screen recordings, writing artifacts, think-aloud and stimulated-recall interviews, and interaction logs.Findings Four interaction modes emerged: Passive Receiver, Active Accepter, Constructive Writer, and Interactive Collaborator. SmartStory users devoted more time to planning and produced narratives with higher mean lexical diversity; StepStory users produced narratives with higher mean referential cohesion and narrativity. Qualitative findings linked active evaluation and adaptation of AI suggestions with stronger narrative integration. Revision remained limited across both conditions.Contribution The findings offer exploratory insights into how children negotiate agency, evaluative thinking, and narrative control with AI. They highlight design trade-offs between vocabulary expansion and narrative coherence and suggest the need for writing tools that support reflective engagement, revision, and student authorship.

item.title: Harnessing the challenges of AI: academic versus emotional reliance on generative artificial intelligence among Pakistani university students, contextualized against Western benchmarks
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
