item.title: Exploring Cognitive Synergy Framework on Computing Students Epistemic Agency in Robotics Education
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
Generative AI can support robotics programming, but students must still evaluate suggestions and justify design decisions. This study examined changes in grit-related learning dispositions and patterns of epistemic activity during instruction using the Cognitive Synergy Framework (CSF). In a mixed-methods study across six West African universities, we randomly allocated 410 undergraduates to CSF-supported or comparison instruction. A categorical-time mixed-effects model analysed 848 Grit in Robotics Programming scores from 351 students across Weeks 11, 13, and 15. Epistemic network analysis examined coded actions from 30 collaborative groups. The reported GRP condition-by-time interaction was significant, Wald χ 2 (2) = 15.02, p < .001. Relative to Week 11, estimated gains were 0.167 points greater under CSF at Week 13 (95% CI [0.059, 0.274]) and 0.213 points greater at Week 15 (95% CI [0.093, 0.333]). With a 0.20-point downward adjustment to imputed CSF scores at both follow-ups, the joint test yielded p = .103. Group-level network trajectories differed by condition (β = 0.09, 95% CI [0.03, 0.15], p = .004). Gains in independent epistemic agency remained untested. Future studies should match instructional support across conditions and assess individual reasoning, evaluative judgement, and knowledge construction on tasks completed without scaffolding.

item.title: The current perceptions of Saudi pre-service teachers towards the integration of artificial intelligence into early childhood education
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
This study aims to examine the current perceptions of Saudi pre-service teachers regarding the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into early childhood education. The study employed an “explanatory sequential mixed-methods research design.” In the first (quantitative) phase, data were collected via a questionnaire from 114 pre-service teachers (students undergoing professional teacher preparation) in the Early Childhood Department at a university in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia. In the second (qualitative) phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted with a purposively selected subsample of these student teachers (n = 18). This qualitative phase was intended to analyze the quantitative findings concerning “AI-based personalized learning”. The results indicate that Saudi pre-service teachers have knowledge and a level of comfort and familiarity with the integration of technology and AI into general education. In terms of pre-service teachers’ perceptions towards the integration of AI in ECE settings, the results also indicate that they perceive AI in ECE as extremely useful. The potential benefits of integrating AI into ECE lie in classroom engagement and personalized learning. However, the results reported some factors that could affect AI integration in ECE, including a lack of experience, training, support, and clear guidance.

item.title: Don't Take the Researcher Out of Research: Perspectives on AI from Qualitative Scholars
item.description:
Journal of Educational Data Mining
In line with the explosion of public, political, and educational discourses around the incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday life, researchers have recently invested a significant amount of time into exploring and theorizing the use of AI in qualitative data analysis. This proposed use of AI creates a theoretical friction with qualitative methodologists who foreground the interpretive (and essentially human) elements of this research praxis. To productively engage with this friction, authors--who span from being more quantitatively oriented to those who are considered Big Q Qualitative researchers--engaged in conversations with one another in a reflexive process of self-study. To help facilitate these conversations, all the authors explored CAILA, a qualitative analysis tool that uses AI to autonomously generate codes and themes from a text-based data set. Authors familiar with the tool spoke to the other three scholars who begrudgingly experimented with CAILA for the first--and last--time. Analysis of these conversations showed that participants felt that AI-based research tools could support menial aspects of qualitative analysis or help with coding of data based on established codebooks. However, the participants also found that tools like CAILA failed to provide meaningful interpretations of the data and stripped the humanistic components of qualitative research from the analysis process. These findings sit in opposition to the purported value of AI software, which emphasizes the efficiency of research processes. To this end, our findings position qualitative research as a human pursuit, asserting that the slow pace of the coding processes provides the space needed for researchers to develop new ideas and meaning from bodies of text. We contribute to the ongoing conversation about using AI for qualitative data analysis by providing fresh perspectives from Big Q Qualitative methodologists and inviting the field to think more deeply about the qualitative research process.

item.title: Perceived AI agreement and teacher support for reasoned dissent in relation to intellectual humility and counterevidence seeking
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction When students feel that generative artificial intelligence (AI) agrees with them, do they remain willing to acknowledge possible error and seek evidence against their own views? We distinguished AI support for an answer from teacher support for questioning an answer. We examined how perceived AI agreement and teacher support for reasoned dissent relate to state intellectual humility and reported counterevidence seeking. Methods We surveyed 386 undergraduates, mainly first-year students, at one vocational and technical university. Students completed the questionnaire in class after an AI-assisted English learning task. A separate pilot sample informed the measurement model. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling examined the associations, with bootstrap intervals for indirect associations. Results In the main model, perceived AI agreement and teacher support were positively associated with intellectual humility. Humility was positively associated with reported counterevidence seeking. The estimated indirect associations involving humility were positive for both predictors. Their bootstrap intervals excluded zero, with no clear difference between the two estimates. Neither direct path was statistically significant in the main model. Discussion These initial findings suggest that perceived support for one’s view and encouragement to question claims should be considered together when examining humility and counterevidence seeking in AI-assisted learning.

item.title: When authorship blurs, responsibility dilutes: a three-wave longitudinal study of human–AI co-authorship ambiguity and self-reported GenAI-related academic behaviors among Chinese high school students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges traditional boundaries of academic authorship, potentially weakening students’ psychological ownership and accountability. This three-wave longitudinal study examined prospective associations among human–AI co-authorship ambiguity (HAAA), psychological ownership, responsibility dilution, and self-reported GenAI-related academic behaviors. Data from 586 Chinese high school students (91.3% retention) were analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to distinguish within-person fluctuations from stable between-person differences. Across both intervals, greater HAAA predicted lower psychological ownership ( β = −0.283 and −0.265) and greater responsibility dilution ( β = 0.251 and 0.230). Lower psychological ownership predicted greater responsibility dilution ( β = −0.291 and −0.275), which subsequently predicted more frequent GenAI-related academic behaviors ( β = 0.332 and 0.347; all p < 0.001). Significant two-lag indirect associations linked HAAA to later academic-behavior scores through psychological ownership ( b = 0.045) and responsibility dilution ( b = 0.077). These findings highlight the importance of authorship clarity, psychological ownership, and personal accountability in GenAI-assisted learning. Although causal conclusions are unwarranted, the results suggest that academic-integrity education should emphasize students’ intellectual contributions and responsibility for AI-assisted work.

item.title: AI leadership readiness profiles and competence gaps among school leaders during digital transformation: a comparative study of China and Kazakhstan
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a school-level governance issue during digital transformation, yet how school leaders translate instructional judgments into implementation readiness remains insufficiently understood. This cross-national study examined AI leadership readiness in China and Kazakhstan, focusing on scenario understanding, instructional value, risk concern, digital leadership self-efficacy, organizational support, leadership support for adoption, implementation readiness, and competence gaps. Methods We analyzed a cross-national quantitative survey of 763 school leaders (China n = 389; Kazakhstan n = 374) using reliability analysis, measurement invariance testing, latent profile analysis, standardized recursive path modeling, and importance–competence gap analysis. Results Internal consistency was adequate for most constructs; AI-related risk concern was lower (α = 0.581, ω = 0.582). Scalar invariance met conventional fit-change criteria, and observed composite scores were higher among Chinese respondents for scenario understanding, instructional value, leadership support, digital leadership self-efficacy, and implementation readiness, whereas risk concern was higher among Kazakhstani respondents. The retained four-profile solution comprised high understanding–high readiness, value-positive–near-average readiness, risk-sensitive cautious, and low understanding–low readiness. Scenario understanding was positively associated with instructional value (β = 0.585); instructional value was positively associated with leadership support (β = 0.339); and digital leadership self-efficacy was positively associated with implementation readiness (β = 0.328). The largest importance–competence gaps concerned ethics and risk governance ( G = 1.75), teacher development ( G = 1.58), and content quality audit ( G = 1.56). Discussion Positive instructional appraisals frequently coexisted with moderate school-level preparation. Implementation readiness was most closely associated with digital leadership self-efficacy, organizational support, and leadership support for adoption. Ethics and risk governance, teacher development, and content quality audit emerged as the leading priorities for professional learning.

item.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

item.title: Redefining efficiency in post-editing of LLM-generated translation: why expert translators take more time
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
This study examines how expertise influences the post-editing of translation generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lens of relevant efficiency—the adaptive regulation of effort in response to task demands, which is operationalized here as temporal regulation, intervention calibration, and resource adaptability. We used keystroke logging and mixed-effects modeling to compare student and professional translators who performed full and light post-editing (FPE/LPE) tasks on LLM-generated translations under structured termbase and open-ended Internet-search settings. The findings suggest that post-editing expertise is not necessarily reflected in faster processing, but in how post-editing behavior relates to task requirements. Experts showed a greater increase in time allocation as the density of critical errors increased, indicating more task-sensitive temporal regulation. Expertise-related patterns of error correction varied with post-editing guidelines, while resource conditions were differentially associated with new-error introduction across the two groups. Keystroke-based process indicators also related to editing outcomes, highlighting the importance of evaluating editing activity in relation to its results. These findings support a task-relative understanding of relevant efficiency in the post-editing of LLM-generated translation, suggesting that translator training should prioritize task-sensitive decision-making, temporal regulation, and effective use of external resources rather than processing speed alone.

item.title: Interactive learning in communication studies amid AI-driven industry restructuring: linking AI-integrated course design to students’ perceived capability development
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
Generative AI is reshaping work and prompting higher education to reconsider course design for changing occupational demands. This study examined associations between AI-integrated interactive instruction and students’ critical thinking, AI literacy, career adaptability resources, and perceived future work readiness. An embedded mixed-methods, nonequivalent-group pretest–posttest design was implemented in a journalism and communication course in China. Survey data underwent ANCOVA, structural equation modeling, and conditional analyses, while classroom records, reflective texts, and interview data were examined through thematic analysis. Students receiving interactive instruction reported consistently higher adjusted posttest scores overall, with the largest difference in AI literacy. The instructional condition was indirectly associated with perceived readiness through critical thinking, AI literacy, and career adaptability resources, whereas its direct association was nonsignificant. The association between critical thinking and perceived readiness was stronger at higher levels of AI literacy, and the condition–AI-literacy association was stronger among students with less prior AI-use experience. Qualitative accounts highlighted comparison, justification, revision, and reflective dialogue as processes connecting course activities with critical judgment, AI-risk recognition, and career-related self-positioning. The findings position perceived readiness as a proximal self-reported outcome and offer a bounded account of how interactive instruction may support responses to AI-driven occupational change.

item.title: Utilizing a GPT-based exam assistant to support practice and assessment in higher education: an exploratory study on learner engagement and perceptions
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Instructors increasingly use chatbots to reduce their workload and to support students with individualized learning opportunities. However, there is still limited knowledge about how students engage with chatbot-based formats for practice and assessment compared to similar human-authored formats. This study examines whether chatbot-supported instruction can achieve similar outcomes with respect to students’ engagement, perceived fairness and perceived usefulness while reducing the workload associated with creating practice and assessment activities. We developed an Exam Assistant (EA) that delivers exam-like open-ended questions, including short case studies, provides immediate feedback, and supports automated scoring with instructor review (human-in-the-loop). The EA was implemented in a real classroom setting with N = 30 undergraduate business students at a German university. Students used the EA for practice and for a graded assignment in the first course phase, while in the second course phase, these activities were delivered via conventional Moodle quizzes. This ensured alignment between practice activities and assessment across both instructional formats . Using learning analytics, chatbot interaction logs from 224 sessions with the EA, and post-assessment surveys, we conducted a descriptive, exploratory comparison of students’ engagement patterns and fairness perceptions. Results show comparably high levels of practice intensity and perceived fairness across both instructional modes. Students demonstrated greater engagement with EA than has typically been reported in prior research on educational chatbots. Nevertheless, students perceived Moodle quizzes as more suitable for future graded assessments, a difference that appears to be driven by question format rather than by fairness concerns. Overall, the findings suggest that thoughtfully chatbot-supported practice and assessment may offer a promising pathway to reduce instructors’ workload without evident disadvantages in student engagement or perceived fairness.

item.title: Attributing Intelligence-Related Capacities to Robots: Perceived Machine Agency, AI Anxiety, and Psychological Distress in Chinese College Students, and the Moderating Role of AI Literacy
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
As generative artificial intelligence (AI) performs tasks once regarded as markers of human intelligence, how people judge the capacities of machines has become a question for intelligence research. This study examined perceived machine agency, the attribution of intelligence-related capacities such as thinking, planning, moral judgment, and problem solving to robots. We tested whether it is associated with psychological distress through AI anxiety and whether self-reported AI literacy moderates this pathway. A convenience sample of 1205 Chinese college students, mainly from Jiangsu Province, completed a cross-sectional survey. Controlling for gender, age, and subjective socioeconomic status, perceived machine agency was significantly but weakly associated with psychological distress. This association was indirect through AI anxiety, and the direct association was not significant. AI literacy significantly moderated the first stage of the indirect association, which became stronger as AI literacy increased. These cross-sectional findings describe associations rather than causal effects. They suggest that attributing intelligence-related capacities to machines is linked to students’ emotional well-being and that greater self-reported AI competence does not by itself weaken this link.

item.title: From psychological needs to knowledge practices: individual inquiry and shared learning in generative AI-supported vocational education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provides rapid access to explanations and examples, but information access does not necessarily become effective learning. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study examined associations among autonomy, competence, and relatedness need satisfaction, knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing, and perceived learning effectiveness. Methods A cross-sectional survey included 300 adult students in computing-related programs at seven vocational colleges in Nanchang, China. The common reference was learning in web design and development during the preceding 4 weeks. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were complemented by fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Results All three psychological needs were positively associated with knowledge acquisition. Autonomy and competence were significantly associated with knowledge sharing; the relatedness coefficient was positive but did not reach the 0.05 significance level. Acquisition and sharing were both positively associated with perceived learning effectiveness. Autonomy and competence had significant statistical indirect associations through both practices, whereas relatedness had a significant indirect association only through acquisition. These separate significance tests do not establish differences between coefficients. Three configurations were associated with high perceived effectiveness, two of which included relatedness. Low-outcome configurations remained exploratory because their proportional reduction in inconsistency values fell below the specified threshold. Discussion GenAI was the contextual framing rather than an independently measured exposure, and the knowledge practices were not exclusive to GenAI. The outcome was subjective, and neither the indirect paths nor the configurations establish causality or objective learning gains.
